newsitem.title: UK: Physical zinc trade dries up in Europe on hot pric.
newsitem.headline: Physical zinc trade dries up in Europe on hot pric.

text.p: A spike in LME zinc prices has dried up physical business in Europe as consumers wait for a correction, traders and industry sources said.
"People are interested but they're not doing anything because they consider the price as being on the high side. If they can wait they do," a trader said.

Three month zinc prices on the LME have shot up nearly $100 to a high of $1,157 since last week, largely on fund short-covering. But chartists say the market is overbought and is due for a correction.
The strong dollar, which has soared to fresh highs this week, has exacerbated the situation.
"Especially in continental Europe where you have the currency factor in addition, it is really expensive," the dealer said.
Some consumers, looking for three month prices to dip at least to $1,100, were becoming nervous in the short-term.
Also bolstering prices and keeping the market tight were falling producer stocks and LME inventories, which dropped on Tuesday by 650 tonnes.
Producer stocks at the end of last year had fallen to their lowest level ever in terms of weeks of consumption, MacQuaries Equities Ltd. said in a report this week.
"At 2.3 weeks of demand, producer stocks have reached rock bottom and producers are increasingly turning to the LME to meet sales requirements," it said.

At the end of 1996, total market stocks, comprising LME and producer stocks had fallen to 929,000 tonnes. This was equivalent to 7.8 weeks of demand and should fall to 7.0 weeks by mid-year, MacQuarie added.
Although tightness this spring might spark some panic buying, many consumers were likely to live hand-and-mouth, betting that supplies would increase from the third quarter, traders said.

As prices rise, mines were likely to reverse cutbacks and increase output, and this plus a seasonal influx of Arctic ore from Alaska and Canada would further help the supply picture, the sources said.

One trader cited the recent sale by Anvil Range Mining Corp of 4.1 million shares to Cominco Ltd to help finance the reopening of the Faro zinc-lead mine in the Yukon, where operations were suspended on December 20.
Cominco markets Anvil's lead and zinc concentrates in Europe.

On the consumption side, orders have risen from the hot-dipped galvanized steel sector over the past several months, but more so in Asia and the United States than in Europe, where economic growth is still sluggish.
Premiums in Europe were holding firm after soaring late last year on the back of news of cutbacks in mine and concentrate output that could deepen a market deficit.
In Europe, duty-paid special high grade (SHG) zinc in Rotterdam warehouse was quoted at $20/$30 over LME cash prices.
Russian material was about $10/$15 below LME cash, but one industry source said not much Russian metal was available in western Europe.
